title: 10500-year-old wooden remains in german lake point to submerged prehistoric settlement
dek: Worked timbers and stone tools emerge from lakebed mud, offering a rare glimpse of Mesolithic activity.
body: About 20 metres beneath the surface of Lake Arendsee in Saxony-Anhalt, underwater archaeologists have pulled up worked timbers, stone tools and animal bones. The finds come from a submerged prehistoric landscape that has been slowly sinking for millennia. Researchers from the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology of Saxony-Anhalt made the discovery during spring 2026 investigations.

Among the most striking pieces is a wooden post roughly 1.6 metres long that still shows the marks of felling and working. Split planks up to 1.3 metres long were also recovered. Scientists suspect the timbers may have belonged to a constructed feature, possibly even a hut. Yet no building plan or other evidence has yet confirmed that the wood formed part of a dwelling.

Describing the site as a permanent settlement remains premature. The artefacts show that Mesolithic people were active at the former lakeshore and were working substantial pieces of timber there. But the duration and nature of that activity are still unknown. Around 10,500 years ago, Central European communities relied on hunting, fishing and gathering rather than agriculture.

Even if a structure is eventually identified at Arendsee, it would not necessarily indicate permanent occupation. Hunter-gatherer groups could build substantial features at camps that were occupied temporarily or revisited seasonally. The real significance of the discovery lies in the exceptional survival of worked wood from the Mesolithic period. Wooden structures from this era are usually known only indirectly, through postholes or soil discolouration.

The waterlogged environment at Arendsee has preserved the timber itself, including traces of prehistoric woodworking. A salt dome beneath the lake has caused sections of the lakebed to subside gradually, submerging former shorelines. Sediment then covered archaeological remains along these ancient shores, creating conditions capable of preserving organic material such as wood. The lake has previously produced discoveries from the Neolithic and medieval periods.

Researchers are now using underwater technology to investigate the prehistoric landscape in greater detail. A remotely operated underwater vehicle, deployed with the Fraunhofer Institute in Ilmenau, has produced high-resolution sonar imagery of the former shoreline. The survey is helping archaeologists identify areas for future investigation and plan more targeted dives. Hopes are high for dendrochronological analysis using the surviving tree rings, though suitable comparative material is scarce.

The timbers are also expected to undergo magnetic resonance imaging in Halle to reveal additional information about their internal structure. Further dives will attempt to establish the extent of the archaeological remains and determine whether the individual pieces of worked wood were connected. For now, the evidence supports the presence of Mesolithic people at the ancient lakeshore, but not yet the existence of a permanent settlement. Determining whether the timbers belonged to a hut, another type of structure or separate activities will be a central question of future research.
doesnt_show: The finds do not yet confirm a permanent settlement or identify the exact function of the wooden structures.
settle: Targeted dives and dendrochronological analysis of the timbers would clarify the structure's function and duration of use.
